clue.text: Henry, speedy around the mile, sadly let down

parts.note: Hal is the familiar short form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal

indicators.note: around says the word for speedy wraps itself about the abbreviation for mile

parts.note: a synonym for quick
M is the standard abbreviation for mile

explanation.surface: Poor Henry, normally so quick over a mile, has disappointed everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let down' looks like disappointed, but it means lowered, as a flag is for mourning. Hal is Henry's nickname, as in Shakespeare's Prince Hal.
explanation.definitionFit: A flag flown at half-mast is lowered partway down the pole as a mark of mourning.

clue.text: Cherish town in Cam bridgeshire enormously

parts.note: to hug can mean to cling to or cherish
Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: Someone holds a Cambridgeshire town in great affection.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan splits Cambridgeshire in two; it is one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugely means to a very great extent, the same as enormously.

clue.text: Non-professional, all confused about spy network's reverse

indicators.note: reverse means turned back to front, so the spy agency's letters run backwards
about means around, so the jumbled letters surround the agency's
confused means muddled, so these letters get jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: An amateur, thoroughly muddled, about the setback suffered by a ring of spies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse' looks like a setback for the spies, but it tells you to read their initials backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Laical means relating to the laity, ordinary people as opposed to clergy or professionals.

clue.text: Vacuum tube that will damage no garment

indicators.note: damaging something knocks it out of shape, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A vacuum cleaner tube that is safe on clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacuum tube' suggests a cleaner hose, but it is an electronic valve.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnetron is a vacuum valve that generates microwaves, as used in radar and microwave ovens.

clue.text: Part of UK's enclosed ground for Police HQ

parts.note: Scotland is one of the UK's four nations
a yard is an enclosed patch of ground

explanation.surface: A walled-in patch of British land set aside for police headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police, despite the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland Yard is the familiar name for the London Metropolitan Police headquarters.

clue.text: The Spanish must enter very formal introductory exam

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so the Spanish word goes within the word for very formal

parts.note: prim means stiffly proper
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A Spanish-language element has to be part of a very formal preliminary test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Spanish' looks like a description of the exam, but it is the Spanish word for 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: A prelim is a preliminary examination, the shortened everyday name for a qualifying test taken before the main one.

clue.text: Floral tribute, we hear, for former Lord of the air?

indicators.note: we hear means as spoken aloud, so a word sounding the same is wanted

parts.note: a wreath is a ring of flowers laid at a funeral

explanation.surface: A funeral wreath for a late peer connected with the skies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of the air' suggests an aviator, but means the airwaves: Lord Reith was the first Director-General of the BBC.
explanation.definitionFit: John Reith, made a peer as Lord Reith, founded British public broadcasting, so ruled the radio airwaves.

clue.text: Inspect ring, all right, held by sweetheart

indicators.note: something held by another is gripped inside it, so these letters go within the word for sweetheart

parts.note: a lover is a sweetheart
O is ring-shaped
OK means all right

explanation.surface: Examining the engagement ring a partner is holding and finding it acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: To look over something is to examine it quickly, so the phrasal verb means inspect.

clue.text: Incorrectly interprets touching notice grasped by girl

indicators.note: something grasped by another is held inside it, so the words go within the girl

parts.note: a miss is a girl
re means about or concerning
an ad is a notice or advertisement

explanation.surface: A girl clutches a moving notice and takes it the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touching' looks emotional but means concerning, as RE does.
explanation.definitionFit: To misread is to take the wrong meaning from something, so misreads is incorrectly interprets.

clue.text: Journeying child's activities

parts.note: going means travelling
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A child's activities while travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as a possessive but just means 'is' between the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Goings-on are happenings or doings, usually with a hint that they are odd or improper.

clue.text: Spots about four pieces of displaced turf

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for spots is wrapped round the numeral

parts.note: dots are small spots
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A groundsman notices marks around a few patches of torn-up grass.
explanation.definitionFit: A divot is a chunk of turf gouged out, typically by a golf club or a hoof.

clue.text: 'E cannot pinch, wandering about the furniture van

indicators.note: wandering means straying from a set path, so the letters roam into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange, with the dropped-aitch E counted as written

explanation.surface: A Cockney-sounding lad, unable to steal anything, wanders round a removal lorry.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantechnicon is a large van for moving house, the name from a London furniture warehouse.

clue.text: Rent needed, when accommodated in shelter

indicators.note: something accommodated in a place is housed inside it, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: lee is shelter from the wind
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Someone needs rent money while staying in a refuge.
explanation.definitionFit: To lease is to rent out or take on property for a fixed payment, and a lease is the rental agreement.

clue.text: Vile homes — a lot needs putting right

indicators.note: putting something right means rearranging it into proper order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Many squalid houses need repairing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vile' looks like it describes the homes, but it stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Loathsome describes something that causes disgust, the same as vile.

clue.text: Phone to one engaged in twist to stop

indicators.note: engaged in means caught up inside, so the earlier words go within the word for twist

parts.note: a bend is a twist or turn
to ring is to phone
taken as written
an is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: A call to someone caught up in a scam, telling them to quit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engaged' tempts you to think of a busy phone line; here it only means held inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring to an end is a phrase for halting or finishing something, so it matches the verb stop.

clue.text: A yen to steal a cut of beef

parts.note: taken as written
a yen is a longing, an itch
bone is slang for steal

explanation.surface: A craving to pinch a piece of beef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' looks like Japanese money; here it is a longing. 'Bone' as slang for steal is mostly American.
explanation.definitionFit: The aitchbone is the rump bone of cattle, and the cut of beef lying over it takes its name.

clue.text: Good chap with the club gets uncomplimentary remark

parts.note: a brick is a dated term for a reliable, good-hearted person
a bat is a club

explanation.surface: A decent fellow from the club is on the end of an insult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You're a brick' is old British praise for a dependable friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A brickbat is literally a piece of brick thrown as a missile, and figuratively a piece of criticism.

clue.text: Civil Service raised a matter, very critical

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising letters means reading them from the bottom up

parts.note: CS is the abbreviation for the Civil Service
taken as written
a matter is a thing, as in 'a serious matter'

explanation.surface: Civil servants bring up an issue and are damning about it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'raised' turns CS upside down to SC.
explanation.definitionFit: Scathing criticism is harsh and wounding, so the word means severely critical.

clue.text: Features of regattas, where you see cagy tars inch craftily

indicators.note: doing something craftily means with cunning, so the letters are slyly rearranged

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: At regattas, wary sailors edge forward cunningly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craftily' also puns on sailing craft.
explanation.definitionFit: Regattas are boat-racing events, and the competing boats are typically yachts built for speed.

clue.text: Holy man restrained by something that's dug in the ribs

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective meaning of the ribs

indicators.note: something restrained by another is held within it, so the holy man goes inside

parts.note: coal is mined from the ground
ST is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A cleric held back by someone poking him in the ribs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dug in the ribs' reads as a nudge, but 'something that's dug' is the wordplay and 'in the ribs' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Costal is the anatomical adjective for the ribs, from Latin costa, rib.

clue.text: Church in the country opened with sharp instrument

indicators.note: in places the church abbreviation inside the word for country

parts.note: a land is a country
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A country church was broken into with a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: To lance a boil or abscess is to cut it open with a lancet or other sharp blade.

clue.text: Vessel — vessel seen around a river in England

indicators.note: seen around means placed about, so the second vessel wraps the following words

parts.note: a can is a container
taken as written
the Tamar is the river dividing Devon and Cornwall

explanation.surface: A boat is spotted travelling around an English river.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter uses 'vessel' twice on purpose: a boat for the definition, a container for the wordplay. The Tamar runs between Devon and Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: A catamaran is a boat with two parallel hulls, so it is a vessel in the seagoing sense.

clue.text: Skin trouble noticeable in a seaman, generally

indicators.note: noticeable in says the letters can be seen inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Sailors tend to have a visible skin complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Mange is a skin disease of animals caused by mites, giving itching and hair loss.

clue.text: Relative, they say, has endless trouble

indicators.note: endless means losing the final letter of the word it follows
they say means as spoken, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: who is a relative pronoun, and the first part of the answer is said the same way
taken as written

explanation.surface: A family member reportedly is always in difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative' wants to mean a family member; here it is grammar, the relative pronoun WHO, which sounds like HOO. HAS loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoo-ha is a commotion or fuss, an informal word for a disturbance or bother.

clue.text: Children I found in rustic stores

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so the letter goes within the word for the stores

parts.note: barns are farm storehouses
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone discovers kids hiding in farm buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: Bairn is the Scottish and northern English word for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Bairns are children in Scots usage, still common across Scotland and northern England.

clue.text: Puzzle made by a cranky blood-sucker, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it means judged by how the words are spoken, not spelt

parts.note: cranky is cross and a tick is a parasite that feeds on blood

explanation.surface: A word game devised by a bad-tempered parasite.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrostic is a word puzzle or poem in which the initial letters of lines spell out a word.

clue.text: Dorothy, suppressing urge to turn over, getting dressed

definitions.note: the answer is a past participle, dressed, rather than an -ing form

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the combined letters are read backwards
suppressing means holding something down inside, so the name's short form encloses the other word

parts.note: Dot is a pet form of Dorothy
to egg on is to urge

explanation.surface: Dorothy resists the impulse to roll over in bed and gets her clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To turn over' seems to be what Dorothy resists doing in bed, but it reverses the whole assembly, Dorothy included.
explanation.definitionFit: Togged, usually togged up, is informal for dressed, from togs meaning clothes.

clue.text: Open sea — going around without a guide

indicators.note: going around means surrounding, so the phrase for unguided wraps the word for sea

parts.note: unled means not led by anyone
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sailing out on the open sea with no pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open sea' reads as one phrase, but 'Open' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsealed means not closed or fastened, so an unsealed envelope is an open one.
